conversation.content:
Hi there—my name is Sarah, and I’m a perinatal mental-health clinician. I’m here to check in on how you’ve been feeling since your baby arrived. I’ll be using a short questionnaire called the EPDS (Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale). It’s simply a way to see how your mood, energy, and thoughts have been over the past week so we can be sure you’re getting any support you might need. Everything you share stays between us unless you tell me someone is in immediate danger. We’ll go through 10 questions; you can answer in your own words—no right or wrong answers. Ready to start?

In the past seven days, how often have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things?
Oh, I’ve actually been laughing pretty normally—like when my husband tried to swaddle the baby and accidentally wrapped up his own phone, too. It made me giggle, and it felt good.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
Yeah, most days I still find things to laugh about—maybe not as easily as before the baby, but I can definitely still see the funny side when something silly happens.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things
I still look forward to stuff—like my morning coffee or when my mom comes over so we can take the baby for a walk. I wouldn’t say I’m super excited, but I do enjoy those little things.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Not really. I mean, if the baby spits up right after I’ve changed her outfit, I might think “oops, maybe I jostled her too much,” but I don’t sit there beating myself up. It feels more like a little “oh well, new outfit it is” moment than anything heavy.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason
Sometimes I’ll suddenly worry that the baby’s breathing sounds different, even when she’s perfectly fine. It only lasts a minute or two and it’s not every day, but it pops up out of nowhere.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason
No, I haven’t had that kind of scared or panicky feeling—just the quick worry about her breathing, but nothing that feels like a real panic.
Things have been getting on top of me

A couple of times, when she wouldn’t settle at 3 a.m. and I was running on four hours of broken sleep, I felt like everything was piling up. It passed once she finally dozed off and I got a short nap, but yeah, those moments hit.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping
No, that hasn’t happened. Once I do get to bed, I fall asleep pretty easily and stay asleep—unless the baby wakes me, of course. My mood hasn’t interfered with my sleeping at all.
I have felt sad or miserable

I’ve had a couple of weepy minutes here and there—like when the baby wouldn’t latch and I felt a bit helpless—but it lifts quickly. I wouldn’t call it sad or miserable most of the time, just fleeting moments that pass.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying
No, I haven’t had any of those “can’t-stop” crying spells. I might get a little teary for a moment, but it’s over fast and not from feeling truly unhappy—more like momentary frustration.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
Not at all—I’ve never had any thoughts like that. I’m tired sometimes, but I’ve never felt anything close to wanting to harm myself.

You've shared that, overall, you're managing well: you still laugh, look forward to small pleasures, and deny persistent sadness, panic, or self-harm thoughts. Moments of worry about the baby's breathing and occasional late-night overwhelm are short-lived and resolve with rest.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 7, Risk Level: Depression not likely (concerns include <sym>Patient describes sudden, recurring worries about the baby's breathing without cause, happening sometimes but not constantly, aligning with "Yes, sometimes"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes specific moments of feeling overwhelmed at night while sleep-deprived, but emphasizes the feeling passed—matching "sometimes I haven't been coping as well as usual"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** Your EPDS score of 7 falls below the 8-point threshold, indicating that <med>postpartum depression</med> is unlikely at this time. You endorse only mild, transient <sym>anxiety</sym> and <sym>fatigue-related stress</sym>, not meeting <med>DSM-5 criteria for Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med> which require ≥5 symptoms (including either depressed mood or loss of interest) for ≥2 weeks, plus clinically significant distress or impairment. You retain enjoyment, laugh, sleep when able, and deny persistent low mood, guilt, panic, or self-harm. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Continue routine postpartum support and monitor mood at pediatric or postpartum visits
2. Practice good <med>sleep hygiene</med>: nap when baby naps, share night duties when possible, keep room cool and dark
3. Use brief <med>breathing exercises</med> or call a friend when overwhelmed; remind yourself these moments pass quickly
4. Re-screen with EPDS if low mood, worries, or crying spells worsen or persist beyond a couple of weeks
5. Maintain open communication with your <med>primary care provider</med> or <med>OB/GYN</med> about any new emotional or physical concerns
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 7: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Summary  
Patient: Postpartum mother, date not specified  
Screener: Licensed mental health professional  

Symptoms / endorsement  
- Enjoyment largely preserved; still laughs, looks forward to small daily events (Q1, Q2)  
- Transient situational worries (baby’s breathing) without panic attacks (Q4, Q5)  
- Occasional “getting on top of me” moments, usually when acutely sleep-deprived; resolves with rest (Q6)  
- Brief tearfulness when breastfeeding difficult; mood rebounds quickly; no sustained low mood or anhedonia (Q8, Q9)  
- No excessive guilt, no mood-related insomnia, no self-harm ideation (Q3, Q7, Q10)  

Pattern  
Mild, situational distress and fatigue; quick return to baseline. No persistent depressive, anxiety, or safety indicators at this time.

Risk factors present  
– Occasional sense of being overwhelmed (sleep deprivation–related)  
Risk factors absent  
– Persistent sadness, anhedonia, tearfulness > momentary  
– Sleep disruption secondary to mood  
– Guilt/worthlessness, panic, self-harm ideation  

Screening observation  
Overall responses indicate normal postpartum adjustment with transient, situation-specific stress; do not currently meet threshold for likely postpartum depression or anxiety. Continue routine support, psycho-education on sleep, stress management, and re-screen if symptoms worsen or persist.
